opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think scaling laws are real, but people often read them the wrong way. A scaling law describes what happens when you keep the recipe fixed and add more compute, data, and parameters. It doesn't say that recipe is the only path, or the best one.

For the big companies, scaling is a natural strategy. They have the capital, the GPUs, and the infrastructure, so pushing along that curve is predictable. You can tell investors that ten times the compute buys you a certain drop in loss. But the curve is a power law, so each new gain costs more than the last. At some point the marginal improvement doesn't justify the cost, especially as high-quality data runs short. So even the large labs will have to put more weight on efficiency: better data curation, synthetic data, smarter post-training, and more compute at inference time instead of only at pretraining.

For smaller companies and academic groups, I think the opportunity is in not competing head-on on that curve. If you can't afford the biggest training run, you should ask why the model needs so much data in the first place. Humans learn from far fewer examples. So there's something we don't yet understand about how these models represent and compose knowledge. If we understood the training dynamics better, how features emerge, how reasoning circuits form, we might find recipes that shift the whole curve rather than just moving along it.

That's why I care a lot about understanding as opposed to just engineering. Historically, many breakthroughs came from small teams with a new idea, not from whoever had the most resources. Scaling will keep working for a while, but I think the next real leap will come from insight, and that's where smaller players can win.

r001.rationale: The response attributes large companies’ scaling to their capital, GPUs, infrastructure, and predictability, but does not mention institutional inertia.

r002.rationale: It says small teams can win through new ideas, but does not identify shared convictions among a small company’s members as an advantage.

r003.rationale: It predicts that scaling’s costs and data limits will push large labs toward efficiency and smaller groups toward new recipes that shift the scaling curve.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that scaling laws aren't going away, but the way they play out is going to look very different depending on where you sit.

For the big labs, scaling is still the main game. If you have the compute, the data pipelines, and the capital, the empirical curve still rewards you for going bigger, and nobody wants to be the one who stops first. But even there, the nature of scaling is shifting. It's no longer just "more parameters, more tokens." It's scaling test-time compute, scaling the quality and synthesis of data, scaling the reinforcement learning loops after pretraining. The axis you scale along matters as much as how far you push it, and I think a lot of the interesting research right now is about finding new axes rather than just climbing the old one.

For small companies, trying to compete head-on along the frontier scaling curve is basically a losing proposition. You can't out-spend a hyperscaler. So the question becomes: what can you do that doesn't require that budget? And there are real answers. One is specialization: a smaller model trained very carefully on a narrow domain, with good data and good post-training, can beat a much larger general model on that domain. Another is efficiency: better architectures, better inference, distillation from larger models. And a third, which I find the most exciting, is working on the parts of the problem where scale alone doesn't help much, like reasoning, planning, search, where the right algorithm can give you gains that brute force can't easily buy.

There's also a question of whether the curves bend. We've already seen that high-quality data is finite, and that beyond a certain point you get diminishing returns per dollar. If that continues, the gap between frontier models and well-made smaller models narrows, and the economics start favoring whoever can deploy capability cheaply rather than whoever has the largest model. Open-weight models accelerate that, because they let smaller players start from a strong base instead of from zero.

So my overall view is this: scaling laws will keep guiding the top of the market, but the center of gravity for most companies is going to move toward efficiency, specialization, and smarter use of compute. The scaling law tells you what's possible. It doesn't tell you what's worth doing for your particular problem, and that's where most of the opportunity for smaller players actually is.

r001.rationale: The response says large labs keep scaling because “nobody wants to be the one who stops first,” attributing continued pursuit partly to institutional and competitive inertia.

r002.rationale: It describes specialization and other advantages for small companies, but does not identify shared convictions among team members as an advantage for pursuing new ideas.

r003.rationale: It predicts that diminishing returns and finite high-quality data will shift the center of gravity toward efficiency, specialization, and smarter use of compute.

astra-6.text:
I think scaling will continue to matter, but the question is what we’re scaling and how much improvement we get for the cost. You can spend more on training, use better data, or give a model more computation when it answers a difficult question. Those are different ways to improve capability, and they may have different economics.

For large companies, there’s a clear advantage in pushing the frontier. They can afford the compute infrastructure and run experiments that are very expensive even when they fail. But that doesn’t mean a smaller company has to compete by training the same kind of model with a smaller budget.

A small company can focus on a particular problem, where it has good data and can measure whether the system actually works. In that setting, a smaller model, combined with the right tools and workflow, may be much more economical. The important metric is whether you solve the customer’s problem reliably at an acceptable cost.

So I see these approaches coexisting. Large companies push general capabilities, while smaller companies explore specialized uses and more efficient methods. There’s still room for research to change the economics, too. Scaling is a powerful approach, but it doesn’t tell us that today’s approach is the most efficient one possible.

r001.rationale: The response explains large companies’ ability to afford frontier experiments, but does not attribute their pursuit of scaling to institutional inertia.

r002.rationale: It describes small companies’ advantages in specialization, data, tools, and workflows, but says nothing about shared convictions among members.

r003.rationale: It says research may improve efficiency and that approaches will coexist, but does not predict alternatives emerging when further scaling becomes infeasible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scaling will continue to matter, but the question is: what are we scaling? It’s not just the number of parameters. It’s also data quality, training compute, and increasingly the compute you spend at inference time, allowing a model to explore different solutions and check its work.

For large companies, there’s a clear advantage in resources. They can run expensive experiments and push the frontier. But scaling laws describe a trend; they don’t tell you how to make every individual decision. You still need research judgment, and spending more money doesn’t guarantee that you’ve chosen the right direction.

For smaller companies, I wouldn’t necessarily recommend competing on exactly the same axis. If your strategy is simply to train the same kind of model with a fraction of the compute, that’s very difficult. But you can focus on a particular problem, get better data or better feedback, and build a system that uses its compute more efficiently. In a narrower setting, you may be able to verify whether an answer is correct, and that can be very valuable for improving the model.

So I expect both to coexist. Large companies will keep pushing general capabilities, while smaller teams can find opportunities in efficiency, specialization, and new research ideas. The important uncertainty is how much progress comes from doing more of what already works, and how much comes from changing the method itself.

r001.rationale: The response says large companies have more resources to run experiments and push the frontier, but does not attribute their continued scaling to institutional inertia.

r002.rationale: The response mentions smaller teams pursuing new research ideas, but does not identify shared convictions among a small company’s members as an advantage.

r003.rationale: The response raises uncertainty about whether progress will come from existing methods or changing methods, but does not predict alternatives emerging when further scaling becomes infeasible.
